slides.title: Collections

blocks.text: A collection is an object that holds and organizes other objects, called elements of the collection
It provides operations for accessing and managing its elements
Many standard collections have been defined over time, such as stacks, queues, lists, etc.
Some collections are linear in nature, others are non-linear

slides.title: Abstraction

blocks.text: Abstraction means hiding the details of implementation.
The interface defines the operations, such as adding and removing the elements of a collection.
A class implements the interface of the collection by encapsulating
(hiding) its private data and implementing its public methods.
A user class interacts with the collection through its interface.

slides.title: A Stack Collection

blocks.text: A stack is a linear collection whose elements are added in a last in, first out (LIFO) manner.
The last element to be put on a stack is the first one to be removed.
In stack terminology, we push an element on a stack, and we pop an element off the stack.
Think of a stack of books, where you add and remove books from the top, but can't reach into the middle or bottom of the stack.

slides.title: Using a Stack: Evaluating Postfix Expressions

blocks.text: Let's see how a stack can be used to help us solve the problem of evaluating postfix expressions.
An infix expression means that the operator is placed between the operands:
<operand> operator <operand>
Example of an infix expression: 12 – 7
A postfix expression is written with the operator following the two operands instead of between them:
<operand> <operand> operator
Example of a postfix expression: 12 7 –

slides.title: Postfix Expressions

blocks.text: When evaluating an infix expression, we use precedence rules to determine the order of operator evaluation.
Multiplication has higher precedence than addition
The postfix expression would be written as

4 5 2 * +
                  * is evaluated before +
Postfix expressions eliminate the need for parentheses
Infix expression: (3 * 4 – (2 + 5)) * 4 / 2 is written as
Postfix expression: 3 4 * 2 5 + – 4 * 2 /

slides.title: Evaluating Postfix Expressions

blocks.text: We'll use a stack to evaluate a postfix expression:
Scan the postfix expression left to right.
When an operand is encountered, push it on the stack.
When an operator is encountered, pop the top two elements on the stack, perform the operation, then push the result on the stack.
At the end, the expression value is the result on top of the stack.
Example: 7 4 -3 * 1 5 + / * evaluates to -14

slides.title: A Generic Stack Interface

blocks.text: We will define our own version of a stack.
We will use a Java interface to specify each method's signature, but without writing its body.
The stack interface is defined as Stack<T>, operating on a generic type T.
The methods of the interface can use the generic type T as the type of some parameters and results.
We will define Stack<T> as part of the mystack package.

slides.title: Managing Capacity

blocks.text: The number of cells in an array is called its capacity.
It is not possible to change the capacity of an array in Java once the array has been created.
What to do if the stack array becomes full?
The push method throws an exception ➔ not good
The push method returns success or failure status ➔ not good
The push operation creates a new larger array to expand the capacity and copy all the array elements ➔ better choice
Creating a larger array to increase capacity is very infrequent, and the user of the stack need not worry about it happening.

slides.title: The ArrayStack<T> Generic class

blocks.text: By convention, collection class names indicate the underlying data structure implementation.
Our generic class will be called ArrayStack<T>
The bottom of the stack will be fixed at index 0 of the array.
An integer variable called top will index the array following the top element in the stack.
The top variable also counts the stacked elements.
If top is zero, then the stack is empty.
If top is equal to the array length, then the stack is full.

slides.title: The push Operation

blocks.text: The push method is O(1) if expandCapacity is not called.
The expandCapacity method is O(n) when n array elements are copied.
However, this method is called only after pushing n elements.

slides.title: The pop and peek Operations

blocks.text: The pop and peek methods are O(1) because the steps are executed once.

slides.title: Exceptions

blocks.text: When should an exception be thrown from a collection?
Only when a problem occurs, which is specific to the concept of the collection.
For example, a stack should throw an exception if the user attempts to pop an empty stack.
However, there is no need for the user to worry about a stack getting full.
The implementation of a stack can take care of allocating more memory to avoid such limitation.

slides.title: Detecting an Empty Stack

blocks.text: A RuntimeException is thrown when a pop or a peek is attempted, and the stack is empty.
Exceptions are classes in Java.
An exception is thrown by creating an exception object.
new RuntimeException("Stack is empty\n");
The exception should be caught by the caller of the pop or peek method.
